title: March online orders
prompt: The digital team reviews the online orders from March 2026. Write `solve(orders)` so it returns the orders placed through the web or the app in March 2026 that weren't cancelled or refunded.
rules: March runs from 1 March to 31 March 2026, and both days count.
Any status except `cancelled` and `refunded` stays in. An order with a missing status, channel or date is left out.
A missing `total` doesn't matter here: such an order still counts.
Return every column of `orders`, unchanged, duplicates included.
hints: There are three separate rules: channel, date and status. Write one condition for each and join them with `&`, each in its own parentheses.
`isin` handles the two channels in one condition, and `~F.col("status").isin(...)` means "not one of these statuses".

March needs two date checks, `>= "2026-03-01"` and `<= "2026-03-31"`. If you write the channels as two `==` joined with `|`, wrap that pair in its own parentheses, because `&` is worked out before `|`.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(orders):
    # Return the March online orders that weren't cancelled or refunded.
    return orders
explanation: Each rule becomes one condition, and `&` joins them: `orders.filter(F.col("channel").isin("web", "app") & (F.col("order_date") >= "2026-03-01") & (F.col("order_date") <= "2026-03-31") & ~F.col("status").isin("cancelled", "refunded"))`. An order with no status drops out even with `~`: the check on a missing status isn't true, and "not" of it isn't true either, so `filter` leaves the row out. A missing total doesn't appear in any condition, so those orders stay. The traps are the month's edges (`< "2026-03-31"` loses the last day, `<= "2026-04-01"` lets in an April order) and `(web) | (app) & (...)` without grouping, which keeps every web order whatever its date or status.
